name: The Pupor Isles
overview: West of the West Lands three arcs of windy, storm-beaten islands curve round an inner sea that the islanders call simply the Pupor, and the islands take their name from it. Their people are seafarers of a Boreal tongue who named the reefs, tides and straits before anyone else; Aenor's First Age ships hired their pilots and copied their reef-names into the first charts, and island ships carried food and wounded for the Grand Alliance where no road could. The plagues of the Second Age emptied whole harbours and let corsair captains take the outer isles, the gales taught the chart-houses to read the names of their drowned each year, and the Necromancer never crossed the wide sea to reach them. Since 4A 702 every crown of Aoaz has sailed by island charts, and since 4A 903 the chart-houses of Adel, Pollos and Raerby have bound themselves by the Pupor Charter. In 4A 1748 the arcs are a crowded sea-world of chart-houses, market isles, broker captains, a sea-king, wreck-right lords, a neutral order of lamp-keepers and corsair havens, poor in land and rich in knowledge, and any fleet that crosses the central sea will need their pilots. Years in the data are one continuous count from the victory of Aen on the proposed lengths of the ages (First Age 1,675 years, Second Age 2,133, Third Age 1,260): 1A 1 is year 1, 2A 1 is 1,676, 3A 1 is 3,809 and 4A 1 is 5,069, so that the campaign year 4A 1748 is 6,816; every entry also carries its date in the Age-and-year form, which is the form the prose uses.

ages.name: The Reef-Names
ages.summary: Island pilots guided the first Aenoran ships through the arcs, and the southerners copied the islanders' names for reefs, tides and straits into their charts; the sea-words of Tritonic were borrowed into every northern tongue with the charts themselves.

ages.name: The Supply Fleets
ages.summary: As Aenor declined the islands traded with whoever came, and when the Grand Alliance gathered against Volgan, island ships kept its armies supplied across the separated seas; the fleet captain Senra of the Pupor Isles is remembered in every chart-house for the supply fleets she brought through. From about 1A 820 the chart-islanders were sworn into one league at the Holy Harbour on the reef shelf inside the arcs, Margorodai, the Sea-Roads, which leased harbours, never conquered land, charged one due to every flag and carried the Grand Alliance's supply fleets under Senra of the Pupor Isles.

ages.name: The Empty Harbours
ages.summary: The plagues of the Long Grief came by ship and killed whole harbours; corsair captains took the emptied isles of the south-west, and in 2A 904 a gale season that sank a third of the fleets of Adel and Raerby began the reading of the Drowned Names. The Grey Breath came first to the league's own harbour, and its fleets carried it to every isle; the harbour was left to its dead and never relit, and the gale of 2A 904 broke its four moles into the reefs of the Cursed Square.

ages.name: The Lamps of the Passages
ages.summary: The chart-houses rebuilt their fleets and quarrelled over reefs, and when a royal Aenoran ship was lost with all hands on the Cursed Square in 2A 1507 the Lamp-House of the Lens was founded to keep the northern passages lit for every ship whatever its flag.

ages.name: The Freight Centuries
ages.summary: Aenor fell to the Necromancer, but the islands lay beyond his reach across the wide sea; they traded with the West Lands and the Cold Lands, Raerby's broker-captains grew rich on freight, and the wreck-right lords of the storm isles grew rich on the gales.

ages.name: The Charts of the Pupor
ages.summary: After the reef-name quarrels Adel's Chart Hall became the copy-house of record, the islanders charted the Pupor and sold the charts to every crown in 4A 702, and the Pupor Charter of 4A 903 bound the chart-houses together while the corsair isles stayed outside it.

countries.name: Adel

founding.story: For four centuries after the restoration of Aenor the chart-houses of the arcs quarrelled over who had first named which reef, until in 4A 388 the chart-houses of Adel island agreed to copy every chart in one house at Sanderz and to record there the first namer of every reef. The Chart Hall became the copy-house of record for all the isles, and the league of Adel's chart-houses grew round it.

roots.story: The chart-houses of Adel descend from the oldest craft of the Boreal peoples. Long before Aen, when the Sunfields still stood in the Cold Lands, the proto-Boreal sailors who went west by sea to the arcs carried words for reef, strait, cape and tide that are older than any chart, and they kept a rule that the chart-houses still swear by: no reef is named until it has been proved by the lead. A pilot who found a reef dropped the sounding lead on it, read the depth and only then gave it a name, and the first namer of a reef was honoured by every sailor who passed it afterwards. When the chart-islanders were sworn into Margorodai, the Sea-Roads, at Halgohavnai in about 1A 820, the league set its chart-office at Adel in 1A 900, and the fleet captain Senra of the Pupor Isles, who brought the Grand Alliance's supply fleets through, is claimed by the Andaios chart-house as its forebear; its strong-room at Sanderz keeps a sounding lead it calls hers. When the Grey Breath ended the league, the chart-office became one chart-house among many, and for four centuries after Aenor's restoration the chart-houses quarrelled over who had first named which reef, until in 4A 388 the houses of Adel agreed to copy every chart at Sanderz and to record there the first namer of every reef. From the lead come Adel's customs: a chart is sworn true by the pilot who sounded it; the Drowned Names are read together with the reefs that took them; and the Chart Hall sells its newest chart to whichever crown it chooses, because the lead belongs to the house that dropped it.

sign.device: A long tapered sounding lead hanging on its line, in lead grey and chart white on deep ink blue.
sign.origin: The sounding lead is the pilot's proof of a reef, dropped before any reef may be named, and the lead the Andaios chart-house calls Senra's hangs in the Chart Hall at Sanderz. The league's chart-office flew a lead on its line over Adel's harbour from 1A 900, and the Chart Hall took it back as its banner when it became the copy-house of record in 4A 388.
sign.meaning: Nothing named until it is proved: to every crown that buys an island chart a promise that it is true, and to rival chart-houses the reminder of who keeps the record.

dynasties.name: The Speakers of the Chart Hall
dynasties.notable: Elected by Adel's chart-houses from the master-pilots; the Andaios chart-house, which claims Senra of the Pupor Isles among its forebears, has given the Hall the most Speakers.

events.name: Proved by the Lead
events.summary: The proto-Boreal sailors who come west by sea to the arcs make their first law: no reef is named until it has been proved by the sounding lead, and its first namer is honoured by every sailor after him.

events.name: The League's Chart-Office
events.summary: The Sea-Roads set their chart-office at Adel, and the Chart Hall that keeps the copy of record descends from it.

events.name: The Copy-House of Record
events.summary: Adel's chart-houses agreed to copy all charts at Sanderz and to record the first namer of every reef there.

events.name: The Charts of the Pupor
events.summary: The Chart Hall finished the charting of the Pupor and sold copies to every crown of Aoaz, and island charts have been the standard of every navy since.

events.name: The Pupor Charter
events.summary: Adel, Pollos and Raerby swore the compact that fixes chart dues, wreck-shares and the protection of pilots; the corsair isles stayed outside it.

rivalries.nature: The corsair haven inside the arcs, which pays tribute to the chart-houses one year and raids them the next.

countries.capitalReason: Sanderz is the best harbour below the Adel Mountains on the sheltered inner shore, the island's richest ground, where the chart-houses first gathered to copy their charts.
countries.today: About three hundred thousand people live on Adel island and its districts under the chart-house league. Whoever sits in the Chart Hall decides which crown gets the newest chart, and in a world at peace the Speaker sells to the highest bidder.

divergence.what: The Chart Hall sells its newest charts to the western courts.
divergence.consequence: The Crossing sails with island charts and pilots and loses fewer ships to the wide sea.

divergence.what: The Speaker keeps the newest charts close and sells to nobody in the war.
divergence.consequence: Every navy sails by old charts, and the island chart-houses become the prize that fleets fight over.

countries.name: Raerby

founding.story: In the centuries when the islands were cut off from Aenor and lived by carrying the West's and the Cold Lands' goods, the shipowners of Ese on the eastern arc grew rich enough to lend ships to others and to settle their quarrels for a fee. In 3A 610 they chose a Captain-Speaker from among themselves to keep the freight-book and the peace of the banks, and Raerby has been an isle of broker-captains ever since.

roots.story: Raerby is the court of the banks. The proto-Boreal sailors who settled the eastern arc long before Aen lived by the great fishing banks of the inner sea, and their first law was the law of the shared catch: when two boats claimed the same shoal, the first great banks-fish taken from it was cut in two before both crews and each took a half, and both fished the shoal for the season. When Margorodai was sworn, the league set its court for the fishing banks at Raerby in 1A 950, and the banks-court judged every quarrel over the shoals of the arcs on the deck of a court-ship anchored over the disputed bank, beginning each case by cutting a fish. After the Grey Breath the court had no league behind it, but the captains of Ese went on settling quarrels on the banks for a fee, and in the centuries when the islands lived by carrying the West's and the Cold Lands' goods they grew rich enough to lend ships to others. In 3A 610 they chose a Captain-Speaker to keep the freight-book and the peace of the banks. From the banks-court come Raerby's customs: a quarrel is settled where it arose, on the water; the freight-book records every hull lent and every share owed; and a broker-captain who keeps the book dishonestly loses the right to judge. The gale season of 2A 904, which sank a third of Raerby's and Adel's fleets, began the reading of the Drowned Names, and the Southern Banks quarrel with Nondondor, open since 4A 1398, is the one case the court has never closed.

sign.device: A great banks-fish of the cod kind, with its fins, chin-barbel and square tail drawn plain, swimming, cut through its middle by a thin white line, in silver on deep bank green.
sign.origin: The cut fish is the first fish of a disputed shoal, cut in two before both crews under the oldest law of the banks, and the league's banks-court cut one at the opening of every case from 1A 950. The broker-captains of Ese kept the cut fish as their banner when they chose their first Captain-Speaker in 3A 610, and the court-ship still flies it when it anchors over a disputed bank.
sign.meaning: An even share, settled on the water: to every fishing crew the promise of a fair judgment, and to Nondondor the reminder that the banks have a court older than its crown.

dynasties.name: The Captain-Speakers of Ese
dynasties.notable: Chosen by the shipowners for as long as they keep the freight-book honestly; the Raeros family of Urbolon has held the office longest.

events.name: The Banks-Court
events.summary: The league's court for the fishing banks sits at Raerby, and Raerby's mediation of the banks is what remains of it.

events.name: The First Drowned Names
events.summary: A gale season sank a third of Raerby's and Adel's fleets, and the chart-houses began reading the names of the lost each year.

events.name: The Freight-Book
events.summary: The shipowners of Ese chose their first Captain-Speaker to keep the freight-book and mediate the banks.

events.name: The Pupor Charter
events.summary: Raerby swore the Charter with Adel and Pollos, and its broker-captains became the keepers of the Charter's wreck-shares.

events.name: The Southern Banks Quarrel
events.summary: Nondondor's sea-king claimed the Southern Banks, and Raerby's broker-captains, who had settled disputes on the banks for centuries, refused to recognise the claim; the quarrel has not ended.

rivalries.nature: The Southern Banks, claimed by the sea-king since 4A 1398.

countries.capitalReason: Ese is the drawn harbour on the eastern arc, sheltered by a pond-lagoon behind the town, where the broker-captains could moor more hulls than any other harbour of the arcs could hold.
countries.today: About a quarter of a million people live on the eastern arc's north with Urbolon and Lemo under the broker-captains. Raerby mediates the banks, hires out ships and watches Nondondor's fleet more closely than any other.

divergence.what: Raerby brokers a sharing of the Southern Banks that Nondondor accepts.
divergence.consequence: The oldest quarrel of the arcs ends, and the islands can face the war at sea as one.

divergence.what: The broker-captains hire their hulls to the Crossing.
divergence.consequence: The West gains a freight fleet, and Raerby gains the West's gold and Aenor's enmity.

countries.name: Pollos

founding.story: Havnai, the great harbour of the western island's north, had always been where island goods changed hands, and in 4A 140 its guild-masters wrote the market law that every buyer and seller in the harbour swears to and set up the strong-room where the chart-houses keep their coin. Pollos has been the market and treasury of the isles since.

roots.story: Havnai has always been where island goods change hands, and the guild-masters of Pollos trace their right to keep the islands' money to the plague that ended the league. When the chart-islanders were sworn into Margorodai at Halgohavnai in about 1A 820, the league's dues, one due from every ship of every flag, were counted into a strong-room at the Holy Harbour that had three locks, and its three keys were held by three captains so that no one of them could open it alone; from 1A 1000 a second strong-room at Pollos held the dues of the western arc. When the Grey Breath came into Halgohavnai, the three key-holders were among the first to fall ill. The key-holder from Pollos was the last of them alive; he carried all three keys home on a ship of the dying, and Pollos has claimed the league's strong-room by survival ever since. In 4A 140 the guild-masters of Havnai wrote the market law that every buyer and seller in the harbour swears to and opened the strong-room where the chart-houses keep their coin, and its three locks are still held by three guild-masters who must turn their keys together. From the three keys come Pollos's customs: no purse of the market is opened by one hand; every coin has been weighed at the strong-room door since 4A 1288, when the guild-masters hanged a ring of corsair coiners on the quay; and the Polai family, who keep the strong-room, are first among the guild-masters because they keep the keys and not because they own them.

sign.device: Three keys hanging from one ring with their bits downward, in iron grey and market gold on deep harbour red.
sign.origin: The three keys are the keys of the league's strong-room that the last key-holder carried home from Halgohavnai in the Grey Breath. They hang on one ring in the strong-room at Havnai, and the guild-masters have flown them over the market since the market law was written in 4A 140; a Pollos merchant's seal still shows three keys, and a bargain sealed with it is good in every harbour of the Charter.
sign.meaning: No purse opened by one hand: to the Charter a promise that its treasury is safe, and to anyone who would rob or debase the market the reminder of the quay where the coiners hang.

dynasties.name: The guild-masters of Havnai
dynasties.notable: The market is ruled by the guild-masters of its trades; the Polai family, who keep the strong-room, have been first among them for most of its history.

events.name: The League's Strong-Room
events.summary: Pollos keeps the strong-room where the league's dues were counted, and still keeps it for whoever pays.

events.name: The Three Keys Carried Home
events.summary: When the Grey Breath strikes the Holy Harbour, the last living key-holder of the league's strong-room carries all three of its keys home to Pollos on a ship of the dying.

events.name: The Market Law
events.summary: The guild-masters of Havnai wrote the market law and opened the chart-houses' strong-room.

events.name: The Pupor Charter
events.summary: Pollos swore the Charter with Adel and Raerby and became the treasury that holds its dues.

events.name: The False Coin
events.summary: A ring of corsair coiners passed false silver through the market; the guild-masters hanged them on the quay and since then every coin is weighed at the strong-room door.

rivalries.nature: The southern half of the same island, whose corsairs the market must tolerate and whose king it must humour.

countries.capitalReason: Havnai is the one great harbour of the western island, on the Pollos Passage between the western and inner arcs, where ships of every arc meet.
countries.today: About a hundred and twenty thousand people live in the north of the western island, with Hesos and Aatah, under the guild-masters. Pollos holds the chart-houses' treasury and sells everything to everyone.

divergence.what: The guild-masters lend the Charter's treasury to one crown in the war.
divergence.consequence: That crown's fleet is paid for a year, and every chart-house asks whether the Charter's coin was Pollos's to lend.

divergence.what: Pollos closes its market to a crown that attacks the isles.
divergence.consequence: The aggressor loses the islands' trade and the islands lose their best customer.

countries.name: Nondondor

founding.story: The southern half of the western island was a nest of corsair captains after the Empty Harbours, until in 2A 760 a captain named Kusion of the Kilai beat the others one by one, hanged those who would not swear and took the title of sea-king at the cliff harbour of Kudaini. He made his corsairs fishers in peacetime and his fishers corsairs in war, and his line is the only hereditary crown of the arcs.

roots.story: Nondondor is the only crown of the arcs, and its crown was made of rope. The southern half of the western island was a nest of corsair captains after the Grey Breath emptied the harbours of the Sea-Roads, and for six centuries the captains fought one another for its coves. In 2A 760 a captain of the Kilai named Kusion beat the others one by one at sea, hanged on their own yards those who would not swear, and called the survivors to the cliff harbour of Kudaini; there being no gold among them for a crown, he had a length of his ship's anchor cable twisted into a ring, set it on his own head and called himself sea-king. He made his corsairs fishers in peacetime and his fishers corsairs in war, and his line has held the cliff harbour since. The Kilai claim more than their island. They say that the league that died in the Grey Breath had one due and one law for every flag, and that a crown is needed to keep both; the claim to the Southern Banks, pressed since 4A 1398, is their first step toward that, and Seite and Raerby refuse it every year. From the rope crown come the sea-kings' customs: the crown passes to the eldest son or daughter who has commanded a ship; every Kilai king is crowned with a cable twisted from his own ship's anchor rope; and a corsair in the king's waters sails by the king's writ or hangs. In 4A 1630, after the burning of Straton, the sea-king hanged forty corsairs who had sailed without his writ, so that the western fleets would not come for Kudaini next.

sign.device: A crown twisted from a ship's anchor cable with its strands showing, in rope tan on deep sea black.
sign.origin: The cable crown is the crown Kusion of the Kilai twisted from his ship's anchor rope at Kudaini in 2A 760, when there was no gold for a crown among the corsairs he had beaten. Every sea-king since has been crowned with a new one twisted from his own ship's cable, and the old crowns hang in the hall of Kudaini; the royal galleys fly the cable crown, and the king's sailing-writ is sealed with a twist of tarred rope.
sign.meaning: A crown made at sea and kept at sea: to the king's captains a promise of writs and plunder in war, and to the corsairs who sail without one the threat of the rope.

dynasties.name: The Kilai sea-kings of Kudaini
dynasties.notable: Descended from Kusion, the first sea-king; the crown passes to the eldest son or daughter who has commanded a ship, and the king grants a sailing-writ to every corsair in his waters or hangs him.

events.name: The First Sea-King
events.summary: Kusion of the Kilai beat the corsair captains of the southern isle and took the title of sea-king at Kudaini.

events.name: The Southern Banks Claimed
events.summary: The sea-king claimed the Southern Banks fishing grounds for his crown, and the quarrel with Seite and Raerby began.

events.name: The Hanging Season
events.summary: After the burning of Straton the sea-king hanged forty corsairs who had sailed without his writ, so that the western fleets would not come for Kudaini next.

rivalries.nature: The Southern Banks, which Seite calls its fathers' banks.

countries.capitalReason: Kudaini is the sea-king's cliff harbour on the island's south shore, which the first king took because its cliffs could not be stormed and its harbour faced the banks.
countries.today: About ninety thousand corsairs and fishers live on the south of the western island and on Melkos under the sea-king. Nondondor presses its banks claim whenever its fleet is stronger than Raerby's, and grants writs or hangs corsairs as suits the season.

divergence.what: The sea-king seizes the Southern Banks by force.
divergence.consequence: The arcs go to war with themselves, and the island fleets are spent before the war at sea begins.

divergence.what: The sea-king hangs every corsair who sails without his writ and joins the Pupor Charter.
divergence.consequence: The arcs are safer than they have been in an age, and the corsair havens of the outer arc stand alone.

countries.name: Fineger

founding.story: The northern isles of the arcs are cold, poor and full of reefs, and their folk lived by kelp, sheep and piloting other men's ships through waters only they knew. In 4A 520 the pilots of the Fineger Islands, Ziza and the Kile Islands met at the harbour of Kapai and chose a Speaker to set the pilots' fee for every ship that enters their waters, and the pilots' isles have kept their Speaker since.

roots.story: The cold northern isles of the arcs are the nearest to the Cold Lands, and their folk are the island kin who kept the most of the old north. Their pilots' words for ice and reef are the proto-Boreal words of the Sunfields, and the pilots say their forefathers came down from the north over the ice when the long winters drove the Sunfield clans out of their halls long before Aen, driving their sheep before them. Their oldest tale is of the first crossing to the Kile Islands: the channel had frozen and nobody knew whether the ice would bear them, until a white ram walked out onto it ahead of the flock and crossed, and the families followed where its hooves had held. The ram that leads the flock over the ice has been the pilots' sign since, and the pilots of the northern isles still say that a pilot is the ram of his ship. They lived by kelp, sheep and piloting other men's ships through waters only they knew, and in 4A 520 the pilots of the Fineger Islands, Ziza and the Kile Islands met at Kapai and chose a Speaker to set one fee for every ship that enters their waters. From the ram's crossing come the isles' customs: a Speaker must have piloted a ship through the Poolho ice; a pilot goes first and is paid first; and a debt is worked off, as the pilots worked off for ten years the grain that Raerby's brokers carried north in the Kelp Famine of 4A 1601. The Norrai Pilotage with the harbour council of Vindael, made in 4A 1466, is the oldest standing compact between the isles and the Cold Lands.

sign.device: A white ram's head with heavy curled horns, in fleece white on ice grey.
sign.origin: The ram is the white ram of the first crossing to the Kile Islands, which walked out onto the frozen channel ahead of the flock. The pilots' isles carved its head on the prow of every pilot boat long before there was a Speaker, and the Speakers of Kapai have flown it over the pilots' harbour since 4A 520; a Fineger pilot boarding a foreign ship hangs a small ram's head of horn at its bow.
sign.meaning: The pilot goes first: to every ship in the northern waters the promise of safe passage for the fee, and to any fleet that would cross without a Fineger pilot the warning of the ice.

dynasties.name: The Speakers of the pilots
dynasties.notable: Chosen by the master-pilots; the Finon family of the Kile Islands has given the most Speakers, and every Speaker must have piloted a ship through the Poolho ice.

events.name: The Ram on the Ice
events.summary: Families driven south by the long winters cross the frozen channel to the Kile Islands behind a white ram that walks out onto the ice ahead of the flock, and follow where its hooves have held.

events.name: The Pilots' Fee
events.summary: The pilots of the northern isles chose their Speaker at Kapai and fixed one fee for every ship.

events.name: The Norrai Pilotage
events.summary: Fineger and the harbour council of Vindael agreed that each would pilot the other's ships through its own waters for a fixed share, the oldest standing compact between the isles and the Cold Lands.

events.name: The Kelp Famine
events.summary: A cold summer killed the kelp beds of the Kile Islands; Raerby's brokers carried grain north on credit and the pilots worked off the debt for ten years.

countries.capitalReason: Kapai, the capes, is the pilots' harbour at the meeting of the northern channels, where every ship coming into the arcs from the north must stop to take a pilot aboard.
countries.today: About eighty thousand pilots, kelp-farmers and shepherds live on the cold northern isles. Fineger's pilots know the northern waters better than anyone alive, and any fleet that crosses toward the Cold Lands or the central sea from the north will need them.

divergence.what: The Speaker hires Fineger's pilots to the Crossing.
divergence.consequence: The western fleets cross with fewer losses, and the pilots' isles are counted among the West's friends.

divergence.what: The pilots refuse every war fleet.
divergence.consequence: Northern waters become a graveyard for fleets that try them without pilots, and the isles' neutrality is tested by whoever loses ships there.

countries.name: Halenor

founding.story: On the storm isles of the outer south the gales throw more ships ashore than anywhere else in the arcs, and in 3A 280 the island chiefs of Halenor swore that whatever the storm brings to a shore belongs to the lord of that shore. Lusai of the Mondon, the first to hold the wreck-right, built the harbour of Sonrale, and her line has argued ever since over whether its lords are wreckers or wayfinders.

roots.story: The storm isles of the outer south take more wrecks than anywhere else in the arcs, and their people have always lived by the gales. Long before Aen, their tales say, the first islanders on Halenor lit fires on the headlands in the gale season to guide the boats of their kin home, and found that the same fires could guide strangers' ships onto the rocks; the shore-fire has meant both things ever since. When the Sea-Roads kept the first lit passages of the arcs, Halenor's shores were lit for the league; when the league died in the Grey Breath, the fires went dark, the wrecks came ashore, and the islanders lived on them. In 3A 280 the island chiefs swore that whatever the storm brings to a shore belongs to the lord of that shore, and Lusai of the Mondon, the first to hold the wreck-right, built the harbour of Sonrale behind a reef that breaks every wave and set an iron fire-basket on a pole at the harbour mouth, empty. Every wreck-lord since has sworn at the shore either to light the shore-fires or to leave them dark. From the wreck-right come Halenor's customs and its quarrels: the storm's gifts belong to the shore; the Lamp-House of the Lens asked Halenor to light its shores in 4A 1068 and was refused, and has never forgiven it; and the wayfinder lord of 4A 1690, who lit the shore-fires every gale season of his life and saved more ships than his forebears had wrecked, is honoured in songs his heirs do not sing.

sign.device: An empty iron fire-basket on a tall pole, in iron black on storm grey.
sign.origin: The fire-basket is the one Lusai of the Mondon set at the mouth of Sonrale in 3A 280, empty, the sign that every wreck-lord chooses whether to light it. The Mondon lords have flown the empty basket since; a lord who swears to be a wayfinder flies it with the basket filled with red cloth for the length of his life, and his heir takes the cloth down again.
sign.meaning: The choice of the shore: to ships in the gale season a question rather than a promise, and to the Lamp-House and every fleet the warning that the shore decides.

dynasties.name: The Mondon wreck-lords of Sonrale
dynasties.notable: Descended from Lusai of the Mondon; the lordship passes to the eldest child, and each lord swears at the shore either to light the shore-fires or to leave them dark.

events.name: The Wreck-Right Sworn
events.summary: The chiefs of the storm isles swore that the storm's gifts belong to the lord of the shore.

events.name: The Lamp Quarrel
events.summary: The Lamp-House of the Lens asked Halenor to light its shores in the gale season; the wreck-lord refused, and the Lamp-House has never forgiven it.

events.name: The Wayfinder Lord
events.summary: A wreck-lord of Sonrale lit the shore-fires every gale season of his life and saved more ships than his forebears had wrecked; his heirs went back to the old ways.

countries.capitalReason: Sonrale is the harbour of the storm isles that the gales cannot reach, behind a reef that breaks every wave, so that the wreck-lords can wait out the storm and go out for the wrecks when it ends.
countries.today: About eighty thousand people live on Halenor, Kilos, Tined, Lunnai and the Surla Islands under the wreck-lord. Each gale season brings wrecks ashore, and each lord chooses again whether to light the shore-fires.

divergence.what: The wreck-lord swears to be a wayfinder and lights the shores.
divergence.consequence: The storm isles become the safest route of the outer arc, and the Lamp-House at last counts Halenor a friend.

divergence.what: The wreck-lord darkens the shores against a war fleet in the gale season.
divergence.consequence: A fleet that tries the storm isles in autumn can be broken without a single island ship leaving harbour.

countries.name: Windy Lands

founding.story: The windward capes of the eastern arc's south take the full force of the gales, and their folk fish from kites and small boats and take whatever the storm drives onto their rocks. In 4A 1010 the cape-lords of Arpos, Sondor, Cheko and Amarelo met at Audailon and swore a league so that no outsider could play one cape against another, and they have kept it, quarrelsomely, ever since.

roots.story: The windward capes of the eastern arc's south take the full force of the gales, and their folk learned long ago to use the wind that tries to kill them. Their tales say that long before Aen their forefathers, Boreal sailors of the first crossings thrown onto the capes by a gale, lived through the first winter by flying kites of sail-cloth from the rocks to catch the seabirds that rode the wind; the kite became their oldest tool and their first prayer, and the cape-folk say the wind is a master that serves whoever holds the line. For ages each cape fought the others and took whatever the storm drove onto its rocks, and outsiders played one cape against another, until in 4A 1010 the cape-lords of Arpos, Sondor, Cheko and Amarelo met at Audailon and swore a league. In 4A 1355 the fishers of the capes learned to fish from great kites flown from small boats, which let them work the windward banks that no other islanders could reach, and the kites went onto the league's banner. From the kite come the capes' customs: a cape-lord holds his seat as a kite-flier holds a line, by never letting go in a gale; the league speaks through one of the four lords each gale season; and whatever the wind brings to the capes is the capes', as the Raerby freight fleet driven ashore in 4A 1590 learned when the cape-lords paid back only a third of its cargo.

sign.device: A diamond-shaped fishing kite with a long rag tail streaming in the wind, in sail white and gale red on sky grey.
sign.origin: The kite is the cape-folk's oldest tool, the sail-cloth kite of the first winter on the capes and the great fishing kite of the windward banks. The kites went onto the league's banner in 4A 1355, when the kite fleet first fished the banks no other islanders could reach; the four cape-lords fly it from Audailon in every gale season, with its tail streaming to show the wind.
sign.meaning: Whoever holds the line holds the wind: to the cape-folk the promise that the league will not let go in a gale, to strong fleets tribute, and to weak ones a warning.

dynasties.name: The cape-lords' league
dynasties.notable: Four cape-lords sit in council at Audailon and choose one of themselves to speak for the league each gale season; the lords of Sondor have spoken most often.

events.name: The Kites of the First Winter
events.summary: Boreal sailors thrown onto the windward capes by a gale live through the first winter by flying sail-cloth kites from the rocks to catch the seabirds that ride the wind.

events.name: The League of the Capes
events.summary: The cape-lords of the windward capes swore their league at Audailon.

events.name: The Kite Fleet
events.summary: Fishers of the capes learned to fish from great kites flown from small boats, which let them work the windward banks that no other islanders could; the kites are on the league's banner.

events.name: The Raerby Wreck
events.summary: A Raerby freight fleet was driven onto the capes and the cape-lords took its cargo by wreck-right; Raerby demanded it back and was paid a third.

rivalries.nature: Neighbours on the same arc, whose wrecks the capes take and whose brokers the capes owe.

countries.capitalReason: Audailon is the windward capes' one harbour with shelter on both sides, where the four cape-lords can meet without any of them sailing into another's waters.
countries.today: About eighty thousand kite-fishers and wreckers live on the windward capes. The league pays tribute to strong fleets, raids weak ones, and never agrees on anything quickly.

divergence.what: The cape-lords join the Pupor Charter.
divergence.consequence: The eastern arc becomes one sea of the Charter, and corsairs lose their last friends on it.

divergence.what: The cape-lords raid the war fleets' supply ships.
divergence.consequence: Every crown that sends ships past the capes must escort them or lose them.

countries.name: Seite Islands

founding.story: The four Seite isles and Mondeluz have fished the same banks for as long as their songs go back, and in 2A 1340 every household of the isles met on the moot isle of Vesko and swore that the banks their fathers fished belong to their children. The isle moot has met every year since, and every household speaks in it.

roots.story: The households of the four Seite isles and Mondeluz have fished the same banks for as long as their songs go back, and their songs go back to the reefs. Long before Aen the first pilots who came to the Seite isles in the first crossings were wrecked on the reefs, and the households say that the grey seals of the reefs bore the survivors ashore on their backs: the reef-spirits came as seals, and the seals are their messengers. No household of Seite has killed a grey seal since, and when the moot raised shrines on the reefs where the first pilots were spared, in 2A 1600, it set a carved seal on each; island pilots of every arc still leave a token there as they pass. The banks the first pilots fished became the fathers' banks, and in 2A 1340 every household met on the moot isle of Vesko and swore that the banks their fathers fished belong to their children. No lord has ruled Seite since: the moot of every household chooses a moot-reader each year to keep its decisions, and the moot-reader stands under the reef-shrine when he reads them. From the seals and the fathers' banks come Seite's customs: every household speaks at the moot; a bank fished by the fathers is never sold, leased or shared without the moot; and since 4A 1398, when Nondondor's sea-king claimed the Southern Banks, the moot has sent his envoys home every year, knowing that its fishers alone cannot hold the banks against his fleet.

sign.device: A grey seal rising from the water with its head raised, in seal grey on reef teal.
sign.origin: The seal is the reef-spirits' messenger of the first wreck, which bore the first pilots ashore. A carved seal stands on every reef-shrine the moot raised in 2A 1600, and the households sewed it on the moot's banner at Vesko; the moot-reader reads the year's decisions under the shrine with the banner behind him.
sign.meaning: Spared by the reef: to every household a promise that the fathers' banks stay theirs, and to the sea-king a refusal sent home every year.

dynasties.name: The isle moot of Vesko
dynasties.notable: No lord rules Seite; the moot of every household chooses a moot-reader each year to keep its decisions, and the moot-reader stands under the reef-shrine when he reads them.

events.name: The Pilots Spared
events.summary: The first pilots to reach the Seite isles are wrecked on the reefs, and the households' songs say the grey seals of the reefs bear the survivors ashore; no household of Seite has killed a grey seal since.

events.name: The Fathers' Banks
events.summary: The households of the Seite isles swore at Vesko that their fathers' banks belong to their children.

events.name: The Reef-Shrines Raised
events.summary: The moot raised shrines on the reefs where the first pilots were spared, and island pilots of every arc still leave a token there.

events.name: The Southern Banks Claimed
events.summary: Nondondor's sea-king claimed the Southern Banks, which Seite counts among its fathers' banks; the moot has sent his envoys home every year since.

countries.capitalReason: Vesko is the moot isle at the centre of the four Seite isles, which every household can reach by small boat in a calm day.
countries.today: About seventy thousand fishers live on the four Seite isles and Mondeluz. The moot keeps the reef-shrines, refuses the sea-king every year and knows that its fishers alone cannot hold the banks against his fleet.

divergence.what: The moot fights for the Southern Banks.
divergence.consequence: A small isle war becomes the arcs' war, and whoever helps Seite earns the Chart-Faith's gratitude.

divergence.what: The moot agrees to share the banks under Raerby's brokering.
divergence.consequence: The fathers' banks are shared for the first time, and the moot argues for a generation over whether it was right.

countries.name: Santon

founding.story: When the plagues of the Long Grief emptied the outer western arc, corsair captains moved into the dead harbours of Santon, Dani and Kusu, and in 2A 130 the strongest of them, Hanei of the Black Sail, took the strait-place harbour of Straton and made the others swear the Ransom Tide law. The outer arc has been a corsair captaincy since, held by whichever captain is best.

roots.story: The corsair captaincy of Santon was built in dead harbours. When the Grey Breath came into Halgohavnai and the Sea-Roads' own fleets carried it to every isle, ships that carried the sick flew black sails, the old sea-sign of the league for a ship of the dead, so that no healthy ship would come near. The outer western arc emptied; Santon, Dani and Kusu were left to their dead, and the captains who took the emptied harbours were men nobody would fight, because they came in under black sails. In 2A 130 the strongest of them, Hanei of the Black Sail, who had taken a plague-ship's black sail for his own and sailed it into the strait-place harbour of Straton, made the other captains swear the Ransom Tide law: a captive ransomed by the next tide-feast goes home under the god of the harbour, and one not ransomed belongs to the sea. The outer arc has been a corsair captaincy since, held by whichever captain is best until a better one comes. From the black sail come Santon's customs: a captain holds Straton by the sword; every captain swears to the Ransom Tide; and a Santon ship raises its black sail only when it means to take a prize, because the sail still means that whoever it comes for may not live. Corogon's fleet and Varnondor's sea watch burned Straton in 4A 1622 after Santon's corsairs took three Corogon grain ships, and the captains rebuilt it within ten years; since the ransom of the consul's son in 4A 1701, Corogon has sworn to burn it again.

sign.device: A black sail, full-bellied in the wind, without ship or mast, on blood red.
sign.origin: The black sail was the Sea-Roads' sign for a ship of the dead in the Grey Breath, flown so that healthy ships would keep away. Hanei of the Black Sail took one from a plague-ship and sailed it into Straton in 2A 130, and the captains of the outer arc have flown it since; a captain of Straton is made by raising the black sail on his own ship in the harbour, and it comes down when a better captain raises his.
sign.meaning: Death comes under it: to the captains the promise of the Ransom Tide's law, and to every merchant who sees it the plain threat of a prize taken.

dynasties.name: The captains of Straton
dynasties.notable: The best captain holds the outer arc by sword until a better one comes; the Ransom Tide law decides who is ransomed and who is drowned, and every captain swears to it.

events.name: The Empty Harbours Taken
events.summary: Corsair captains took the plague-emptied harbours of the outer western arc, and Hanei of the Black Sail held Straton.

events.name: The Burning of Straton
events.summary: After Santon's corsairs took three Corogon grain ships, Corogon's fleet and Varnondor's sea watch burned Straton; the captains rebuilt it within ten years and have not raided Corogon's grain since.

events.name: The Ransom of the Consul's Son
events.summary: Santon's corsairs took a son of Corogon's consuls at sea and ransomed him under the Ransom Tide law for his weight in silver; the consuls paid, and swore to burn Straton again one day.

rivalries.nature: The consulate that burned Straton in 4A 1622.
The sea watch that hunts the outer arc's corsairs.

countries.capitalReason: Straton, the strait-place, commands the narrows between Santon and Dani, where every ship from the Santon Sea into the arcs must pass under the corsairs' cliffs.
countries.today: About sixty thousand corsairs and their families live on Santon, Dani and Kusu facing the Santon Sea. The captains raid weak merchant fleets, pay tribute to strong ones and remember that Corogon has sworn to burn Straton again.

divergence.what: Santon's corsairs prey on the western fleets in the last war.
divergence.consequence: Western ships carrying men home from the war are taken under the Ransom Tide law, and the West's grudge turns on the islands.

divergence.what: A crown takes Santon's corsairs into its pay as its own raiders.
divergence.consequence: The outer arc becomes a fleet in that crown's service, and the corsairs' enemies become that crown's enemies.

countries.name: Benan

founding.story: The Benan Mountains rise in the middle of the long western island with coves under them that no fleet can find without a Benan pilot, and in 2A 980 a captain named Urai the Lame made the cove of Torni a haven for every corsair who would pay its dues and keep its peace. Benan holds the Cursed Square as its own in name, because nobody else wants it, and its captains keep the haven still.

roots.story: Benan holds the reefs where the Sea-Roads died and will not go near them. Halgohavnai, the Holy Harbour of Margorodai, stood on the reef shelf inside the arcs, a harbour where any ship of any flag paid one due; the Grey Breath came into it first and it was left to its dead and never relit, and the gale season of 2A 904 broke its four moles into the square of reefs that wrecks ships, the Cursed Square. The corsairs of the Benan Mountains, whose coves no fleet can find without a Benan pilot, claimed the Square in 2A 925 because nobody else wanted it, and none of them has ever sailed into it. In 2A 980 a captain named Urai the Lame made the cove of Torni a haven for every corsair who would pay its dues and keep its peace. The haven's captains say Urai taught that a corsair is a crab in a borrowed shell, living in harbours other men built and leaving when a bigger crab comes, and that the one shell a crab must never crawl into is the one its owner died in. When a royal Aenoran ship was lost with all hands on the Square in 2A 1507, Benan's corsairs took nothing from the wreck, and they have refused to sail into the Square since. From the borrowed shell come Torni's customs: the haven chooses its captain from those who pay its dues; the haven's peace and the Ransom Tide are kept inside the cove; nothing is taken from the Square; and the chart-houses' tribute, paid since 4A 1480, buys peace only as long as it is paid on time.

sign.device: A hermit crab in a spiral shell with its claws raised, in shell white and crab red on cove black.
sign.origin: The crab in the borrowed shell is Urai the Lame's saying, made into a banner when he opened the haven at Torni in 2A 980: corsairs live in shells other men built. The haven's captains have flown it over the hidden cove since, and a corsair who pays the haven's dues is given a small shell to hang at his masthead, which every Benan pilot respects.
sign.meaning: We live in what others left: to the corsairs a promise of the haven's peace, to the Charter the reminder that Benan holds the Square in name, and to every captain the warning never to crawl into a dead man's shell.

dynasties.name: The captains of Torni
dynasties.notable: The haven chooses its captain from the corsairs who pay its dues; the captain keeps the haven's peace and the Ransom Tide law.

events.name: The Square Held in Name
events.summary: Benan's captains claim the reefs of the Cursed Square after the gale breaks the old moles, and none of them ever sails into it.

events.name: The Haven at Torni
events.summary: Urai the Lame opened the cove of Torni as a haven for corsairs who would pay its dues and keep its peace.

events.name: The Wreck of the Square
events.summary: A royal Aenoran ship was lost with all hands on the Cursed Square; Benan's corsairs took nothing from it and have refused to sail into the Square since.

events.name: The Tribute Years
events.summary: The chart-houses paid Benan a yearly tribute to keep its corsairs off Charter ships, and Benan took it and raided anyway whenever the tribute was late.

rivalries.nature: The chart-houses who pay Benan tribute and hunt its corsairs at the same time.

countries.capitalReason: Torni is a cove under the Benan Mountains whose entrance cannot be seen from the sea, the safest haven inside the arcs for ships that do not want to be found.
countries.today: About fifty thousand people live in the Benan Mountains, on Bono and in the coves, under the haven's captain. The corsairs take tribute from the Charter and raid when it is late, and they keep well away from the Cursed Square.

divergence.what: The Pupor Charter buys Benan into its compact for good.
divergence.consequence: The haven inside the arcs becomes a Charter harbour, and the inner sea is safe for the first time since the Empty Harbours.

divergence.what: Benan opens its haven to a war fleet hunting the islands.
divergence.consequence: An enemy can lie hidden inside the arcs, and no chart-house harbour is safe.

countries.name: The Lens

founding.story: When a royal Aenoran ship was lost with all hands on the Cursed Square in 2A 1507, the glass-blowers of the round isle of the Lens swore themselves an order to keep the northern passages lit, for every ship whatever its flag. The first Keeper, Saneros of the glass-house, built the great lamp-tower at Lighon, and every chart-house of the arcs has paid lamp-dues to the order since.

roots.story: The round isle of the Lens keeps the league's light. The proto-Boreal sailors who first came to the arcs long before Aen kept fires on the capes to guide one another through the passages, and the Sea-Roads made of them the first lit passages of Aoaz: towers on the capes of the northern passages whose lamps any ship of any flag might steer by for one due. When the Grey Breath ended the league, the lamps went dark one by one, and for more than a thousand years the northern passages were unlit. In 2A 1507 a royal Aenoran ship was lost with all hands on the Cursed Square, and the glass-blowers of the round isle, who had made the lamp-glass of the old towers, swore themselves an order to keep the northern passages lit for every ship whatever its flag. Their first Keeper, Saneros of the glass-house, blew the great lamp-glass of Lighon in one breath, the order says, and built the great lamp-tower there, and the Keepers say the lamp they relit was the league's own. From the oath come the order's customs: a Keeper is chosen from those who have kept a tower alone through a whole gale season; the Keeper swears never to take a side in any quarrel of the arcs; every Keeper blows one lamp-glass at his oath; and every chart-house of the arcs pays lamp-dues to the order. Since 4A 1544, when Nondondor's ships tried to put out a lamp to wreck a Raerby fleet and every chart-house refused the sea-king's charts for a year, no realm of the arcs has touched a lamp.

sign.device: A long glass-blower's pipe with a round glowing gather of glass at its tip, in pale lamp gold and pipe black on deep night blue.
sign.origin: The blowpipe and its gather are the moment the first Keeper, Saneros, blew the great lamp-glass of Lighon in one breath in 2A 1507. The order took it for its sign when it swore to keep the passages lit, and every Keeper since has blown a lamp-glass at his oath; the order's banner flies on every tower it keeps, and a ship that flies it is the order's and is touched by no one.
sign.meaning: One light for every flag: to every ship a promise of the lit passages, and to every realm of the arcs the reminder that whoever darkens a lamp loses the good will of every chart-house.

dynasties.name: The Keepers of the Lamp-House
dynasties.notable: The order chooses its Keeper from the lamp-keepers who have kept a tower through a whole gale season alone; the Keeper swears never to take a side in any quarrel of the arcs.

events.name: The Lamp-House Sworn
events.summary: The glass-blowers of the Lens swore their order after the Wreck of the Square and built the great lamp-tower at Lighon.

events.name: The League's Light
events.summary: The Lamp-House relights the old lights of the passages after the Wreck of the Square, and its keepers say its lamp was the league's own.

events.name: The Lamp Quarrel
events.summary: The order asked the wreck-lords of Halenor to light their shores in the gale season and was refused.

events.name: The Neutral Lamps
events.summary: When Nondondor's ships tried to put out a lamp to wreck a Raerby fleet, every chart-house refused the sea-king's charts for a year, and since then no realm of the arcs has touched a lamp.

countries.capitalReason: Lighon, the bright harbour, sits under the great lamp-tower on the round isle, which stands where the northern passages meet and where a light can be seen from all of them.
countries.today: About twenty thousand lamp-keepers and glass-blowers live on the round isle. The order keeps the lamps of the northern passages, takes no side in any feud, and any realm that attacks the Lens loses the good will of every chart-house of the arcs.

divergence.what: The Keeper darkens the lamps to stop a war fleet entering the arcs.
divergence.consequence: The passages become deadly for every ship including the islanders' own, and the order's oath of neutrality is broken for the first time.

divergence.what: A crown seizes the Lens to control the passages.
divergence.consequence: That crown holds the lights of the north and loses the friendship of every chart-house of the arcs.

cities.name: Sanderz
cities.legend: The chart-masters of Sanderz say that the first reef ever charted in the arcs is drawn on the wall of the Chart Hall's oldest room, and that a pilot who cannot name it may not be called a master.
cities.economy: The Chart Hall: charts copied and sold to every crown, pilots, timber and fish.

cities.name: Lusticos
cities.legend: Shepherds of the Zuman Uplands say the green upland was a reef once, raised from the sea so that the islanders would have one field of good grass.
cities.economy: Sheep, wool, oats and beans on the uplands' shore.

cities.name: Ese
cities.legend: The broker-captains say the pond beside Ese was dug by the first captain to hide his ships from a corsair fleet, and that it has never since held fewer than ten hulls.
cities.economy: Freight and brokerage, ships for hire and the banks mediation.

cities.name: Havnai
cities.legend: The guild-masters say that every coin that has passed through Havnai's market since the False Coin has been weighed at the strong-room door, and that the scales have never been wrong.
cities.economy: The market of the isles and the chart-houses' strong-room.

cities.name: Kudaini
cities.legend: Corsairs of Kudaini say the first sea-king hanged the last captain who refused him from the cliff above the harbour, and that the rope still hangs there for the next one.
cities.economy: The sea-king's harbour, fishing and corsairing under the king's writ.

cities.name: Kapai
cities.legend: The pilots of Kapai say that a pilot who has seen the Poolho ice break in spring will never be lost at sea, and every apprentice is taken north to watch it.
cities.economy: Pilots' fees, kelp, sheep and the northern channels.

cities.name: Sonrale
cities.legend: The wreck-lords of Sonrale keep a bell from every ship the storm has given them, and the islanders say the bells ring of themselves before a great gale.
cities.economy: Wreck-right, salvage, fishing and storm-isle sheep.

cities.name: Straton
cities.legend: The corsairs of Straton say the town has been burned twice and rebuilt twice, and that the third burning will be Corogon's last mistake.
cities.economy: Corsairing, ransom under the Ransom Tide law, and fishing.

cities.name: Torni
cities.legend: Benan's pilots say the cove of Torni cannot be found by a man who has not been born on the island, and that strangers who sail into it by chance are not allowed to sail out.
cities.economy: The corsair haven: dues, repairs and stolen cargoes sold quietly.

cities.name: Lighon
cities.legend: The lamp-keepers say the great lamp of Lighon has not gone out since the night it was first lit, and that the night it does, the passages will take a ship for every year it burned.
cities.economy: The Lamp-House, glass-blowing and the lamp-dues of every chart-house.

cities.name: Vesko
cities.legend: The households of Vesko say the reef-shrine at the moot isle was built where the first Seite pilot was spared by the sea, and that a moot-reader who reads a false decision there will be drowned within the year.
cities.economy: Fishing the banks, the isle moot and the reef-shrines.

cities.name: Audailon
cities.legend: The cape-lords say the league's kite banner was sewn from the sails of the first kite boat, and that the league will last as long as it flies.
cities.economy: Kite-fishing, wreck-taking and the cape-lords' council.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Drowned Names
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Since the gale season of 2A 904 every chart-house reads the names of the year's drowned at the close of the gale season, and a pilot's name read there is copied into the Chart Hall's book.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Pupor Charter
lawsAndCustoms.summary: The chart-houses' compact of 4A 903 fixes chart dues and wreck-shares, protects pilots in every harbour of its members and keeps its treasury at Pollos; the corsair isles stand outside it.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The wreck-right
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Whatever the storm brings to a shore belongs to the lord of that shore, and he may choose whether to light the shore-fires or leave them dark.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Ransom Tide law
lawsAndCustoms.summary: A captive ransomed stands under the god of the harbour and goes home; one not ransomed by the next tide-feast belongs to the sea, and every corsair captain swears to this law.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The lamp-dues and the lamp-peace
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Every chart-house pays the Lamp-House for the lights of the northern passages, and since 4A 1544 no realm of the arcs touches a lamp.
